name: Hooke names the cell
scope: The 1665 book that made the invisible world famous, and the word it left us. T1: Robert Hooke shaved a sliver off a cork bottle-stopper, put it under his microscope, and found it was not solid at all -- it was a honeycomb of tiny empty boxes; the bare little rooms monks slept in gave him the name he wrote down: CELLS. T2 (invert the wonder): he did not just look, he COUNTED -- about sixty boxes in a line one-eighteenth of an inch long, which he multiplied out to 1,259,712,000 cells in a single cubic inch of cork; the astonishing number goes in the stem, the humble material (cork) is what must be known. T3 (the correction rung): Hooke was looking at DEAD wood -- what he saw were only the empty walls left behind; the living contents of a cell were not what he found, and he never knew cells were alive. T4: Micrographia (January 1665) was the Royal Society's first great book, and its selling point was the fold-out engravings -- the flea and the louse plates opened out far wider than the page itself. T5: buried in it is Observation XX, Hooke's drawing of the blue mould on leather -- the first published picture of a microorganism -- which he guessed grew out of rotting matter itself, the very wrong idea Pasteur would later have to kill. T6: Samuel Pepys wrote in his diary that he sat up reading it until two in the morning and called it the most ingenious book that ever he read in his life -- the first science bestseller. T7 (mechanism): his compound microscope managed only about 30x with bad colour-fringing, so his real edge was LIGHT -- he focused a lamp through a brine-filled glass globe and drew the same specimen again and again under different lighting. T8: Micrographia was not only biology -- in the same volume Hooke argued light travels as waves and that fossils are the remains of once-living things.
source: Grokipedia: Micrographia, Robert Hooke, Cell theory, Microscopy, Timeline of microscope technology; Wikipedia: Micrographia; roberthooke.org.uk transcription of Observation XVIII (cork), which carries Hooke's own 1,166,400-per-square-inch and 1,259,712,000-per-cubic-inch arithmetic; Royal Society print archive (cork plate); Nature Sci. Rep. 2019, 'Four hundred years of cork imaging'.
framing_note: DISCOVERY mode; the naming moment is the hook, never a date question. THE ACCURACY RAIL: Hooke did NOT discover living cells or cell theory -- he named empty dead cell walls in cork; any stem implying he found the living unit of life is wrong and must be rewritten. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (a billion boxes in a sugar-cube of cork). Anti-restatement: never say 'he compared them to monks' rooms' in a stem that then asks what he named them. Distractor mine: real adjacent microscopists and their real claims -- Leeuwenhoek (animalcules, not cork), Nehemiah Grew and Malpighi (plant anatomy, same decade), the Janssens (the instrument), plus the live wrong idea that he saw the cells' living contents.

name: Leeuwenhoek's animalcules and the Royal Society's verification
scope: An amateur cloth merchant sees a world nobody believes -- and the Society makes him prove it. T1: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek sold cloth in Delft and used magnifying lenses to count threads; when he turned one on a drop of lake water he found it crawling with things he called dierkens, 'little animals' -- an entire living world in water people drank. T2 (the payoff): in 1683 he scraped the white film off his own teeth, looked, and drew the wriggling shapes -- the first drawings of bacteria ever made -- reporting that there were more animals in the scum of one man's teeth than there are men in a whole kingdom. T3 (replication as the test): the Royal Society did not simply believe him. Skeptics said no such creatures existed, so Leeuwenhoek sent sworn statements from Delft witnesses (including a notary and local ministers) who had looked through the lens themselves, and the Society ordered Robert Hooke to reproduce the observation -- Hooke's microscopes failed him at first, and only on 15 November 1677 did he finally see the little animals and confirm the claim. T4 (mechanism): his instruments were not the multi-lens compound microscopes of his rivals -- each was a single bead of glass clamped in a brass plate the size of a matchbox, pressed right up against the eye; surviving examples reach about 275x, far beyond Hooke's 30x. T5: he would not tell anyone how he made them -- he showed visitors his poorer instruments and let them assume that was his method, and the secret died with him in 1723. T6 (the modern rung): in 2021 a team at TU Delft and Rijksmuseum Boerhaave fired NEUTRONS through a sealed Leeuwenhoek microscope to image the lens without opening the instrument -- and the celebrated secret turned out to be a blown glass globule made by a technique Robert Hooke himself had published; the advantage was never a magic lens, it was patience, specimen preparation and lighting. T7: in his will he sent 26 of his microscopes to the Royal Society in London; they were subsequently lost. T8: across roughly fifty years he wrote about 560 letters, all in Dutch, describing red blood corpuscles, muscle fibre and sperm -- and his final letters described the symptoms of the illness that was killing him, dictated so doctors could study it.
source: Grokipedia: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, Animalcule, Bacteria, Protistology; Wikipedia: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek; Cocquyt et al., 'Neutron tomography of Van Leeuwenhoek's microscopes', Science Advances, 14 May 2021 (and TU Delft / Rijksmuseum Boerhaave releases); Lane, 'The unseen world: reflections on Leeuwenhoek (1677) Concerning little animals', Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (PMC4360124).
framing_note: DISCOVERY plus the bank's soul-rung on REPLICATION -- T3 is why this ladder exists: an extraordinary claim was checked by outsiders before it was believed, and that is what makes it science rather than testimony. ACCURACY RAIL: single-lens, NOT a compound microscope, and he did not invent the microscope -- both are common textbook errors and both make excellent distractors. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the teeth). Anti-restatement: describe the SCENE (a draper, a drop of pond water, disbelieving fellows in London) and let the identity of the man or the substance be recalled knowledge. Distractor mine: Hooke, Swammerdam, Malpighi, Redi -- real contemporaries doing real adjacent work -- plus the two live misconceptions above.

name: All cells from cells -- and the man who got no credit
scope: How the unifying claim of biology was assembled, mechanism-wrong first. T1: in 1838-39 Matthias Schleiden (plants) and Theodor Schwann (animals) put forward one claim that covered an oak, a frog and a boy -- every living thing is built of cells; the same brick everywhere. T2 (the wrong mechanism): they thought new cells CRYSTALLISED out of a structureless juice they called cytoblastema, the way sugar crystals grow in syrup -- a tidy idea that was completely wrong. T3: Robert Remak actually watched it happen instead -- following red blood cells in chick embryos and then frog eggs just after fertilisation through the 1850s, he saw existing cells pinch in two; cells come from cells dividing, not from juice condensing. T4: Rudolf Virchow's 1855 slogan omnis cellula e cellula -- every cell from a cell -- is the line every textbook quotes, and Remak's name is not in most of them; historian Paul Weindling documents the priority claim against Virchow, and Remak, a Jew in Prussia, was refused a full professorship for most of his working life. T5 (what the slogan really means): if no cell has ever formed from non-living stuff since, then every one of your thirty-odd trillion cells sits at the end of an unbroken chain of divisions running back through your mother and every ancestor to the earliest cells on Earth. T6 (the honest gap): the rule is a rule about now -- the FIRST cell had to come from non-cellular chemistry, and how that happened is still unsolved; the bank says nobody yet knows. T7: the slogan was not even new -- Francois-Vincent Raspail had printed the same Latin phrase in 1825, thirty years before Virchow made it famous.
source: Grokipedia: Cell theory, Matthias Jakob Schleiden, Theodor Schwann, Cell (biology); Wikipedia: Robert Remak (incl. the Weindling priority claim and the Prussian professorship refusal); Ribatti, 'The Cellular Theory' (PMC6108677).
framing_note: DISCOVERY plus a credit-and-institution rung. ACCURACY RAIL: do not let a rung call Virchow the discoverer that cells divide -- Remak demonstrated it and Raspail had already coined the phrase; equally, do not overclaim fraud: 'plagiarised' is a historian's characterisation, so state the documented facts (Remak's observations came first, Virchow's slogan carried the credit). Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the unbroken chain back to the first cell). Anti-restatement: for the T2 rung set the scene as 'the mechanism they proposed was wrong' without naming crystallisation before asking for it. Distractor mine: cytoblastema and spontaneous generation (the live wrong theories), and real adjacent discoveries of the same decades -- Brown naming the nucleus (1831), Purkinje's 'protoplasm', Dujardin's 'sarcode'.

name: Pasteur's swan-neck flask
scope: The experiment that killed spontaneous generation -- and the single move that made it undeniable. T1 (the kid-replicable heart): Pasteur boiled broth in flasks whose necks he had drawn out into long S-curves left WIDE OPEN to the air; months passed and the broth stayed clear -- then he tipped a flask so the broth ran into the dust caught in the bend, and it clouded within a day. Same air, same broth: the dust was the difference. T2: what serious people believed was that life arose from matter itself, and Felix Pouchet, director of the Rouen natural history museum, had run careful experiments that appeared to demonstrate exactly that. T3: the French Academy of Sciences hung a bounty on the question -- the Alhumbert Prize of 2,500 francs -- and Pasteur took it in 1862; a public prize as a device for forcing a decisive test. T4 (the field test): Pasteur carried sealed sterile flasks up into the mountains and broke them open at different altitudes -- nearly all the flasks opened in a courtyard spoiled, eight of twenty on the Jura plateau, and on the Mer de Glace glacier at about 2,000 m only ONE of twenty went cloudy; cleaner air, fewer spoiled flasks, exactly as dust-borne germs predict. T5 (fairness to the loser): Pouchet was not a fraud and not careless -- his hay infusions happened to carry heat-resistant bacterial spores that survived his boiling, so his flasks really did grow life after 'sterilisation'; the spores were not discovered until later. T6: at the Sorbonne in 1864 Pasteur declared that the doctrine of spontaneous generation would never recover from the mortal blow of this simple experiment -- and the swan-neck flasks he sealed are still sitting clear and uncontaminated at the Institut Pasteur. T7: he was not first to try -- Francesco Redi's gauze over meat (1668) stopped maggots, and Spallanzani and Needham had fought to a draw over sealed broths a century before Pasteur found the shape of neck that answered every objection.
source: Grokipedia: Louis Pasteur, Spontaneous generation; Wikipedia: Louis Pasteur, Spontaneous generation; Institut Pasteur history pages ('The middle years 1862-1877'); Wellcome Collection M0012525 'Three flasks opened by Pasteur in various localities'; Carl Zimmer, 'Louis Pasteur's relentless hunt for germs floating in the air' (2025).
framing_note: REVERSAL mode with a genuinely home-testable core (a jar of broth, a curved straw). ACCURACY RAIL: this ladder is about SPONTANEOUS GENERATION ONLY -- it does not prove the germ theory of disease, and no rung may say it did. Second rail: give Pouchet his due; the spore explanation is the honest reason he saw what he saw. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (the tilt). Anti-restatement: describe the two flasks and the tilt, and let the conclusion be the recalled knowledge -- never announce 'germs come from the air' in the stem. Distractor mine: the real live alternatives of the 1860s -- a vital force in the air, the broth being 'used up' or losing oxygen when boiled, the heat destroying the broth's fertility -- plus Needham and Pouchet as real rival scientists.
history_overlap: COOKING bank owns pasteurisation as a kitchen/food-safety process and may already carry Pasteur facts there -- this ladder must key the FLASK and spontaneous generation, never milk or wine spoilage as a cooking process. Within the science bank, a medicine/germ-theory sub-strand owns Pasteur's rabies vaccine and germ theory of disease; keep those out of this ladder.

name: Lynn Margulis: your cells run on captured bacteria
scope: The rejected paper that turned out to be the textbook. T1: the little power plants inside every one of your cells were once free-living bacteria that got swallowed and never digested -- an idea Lynn Sagan (later Lynn Margulis) published in 1967 after, by her own account, about fifteen journals had turned the paper down. T2 (the first tell-tale): mitochondria carry their OWN DNA, and it is a bacterial-style closed loop -- in humans about 16,500 bases carrying 37 genes -- sitting inside a cell that keeps its main library somewhere else entirely. T3: they are never built from scratch by the cell; new ones appear only when an existing mitochondrion pinches in two, the way bacteria divide. T4 (the consequence you can feel): their protein factories are the bacterial 70S type, not the eukaryotic kind, which is why certain antibiotics that target bacterial ribosomes can also poison human mitochondria -- an ancient ancestry with a modern side effect. T5: the same story runs twice -- chloroplasts descend from a swallowed cyanobacterium roughly 1.6 billion years ago, so the green machinery in every leaf and every blade of grass is also a captive. T6 (the open question): which bacterium exactly? Mitochondria sit inside the Alphaproteobacteria, but whether the closest living relatives are the Rickettsiales or the ocean-dwelling Pelagibacterales is still argued -- nobody yet knows. T7 (the host): in 2015 deep-sea mud near the Loki's Castle vents yielded genomes of Asgard archaea carrying proteins previously thought uniquely eukaryotic, and in 2020 a Japanese team finally GREW one -- Prometheoarchaeum, coaxed out of Nankai Trough sediment over more than a decade of cultivation -- and watched it put out long branching protrusions. T8: the idea had been proposed and ignored before -- Konstantin Mereschkowski argued for symbiogenesis in 1905 and Ivan Wallin for bacterial origins of mitochondria in 1927; the same claim was rejected twice, sixty years apart. T9 (it is still happening): the amoeba Paulinella swallowed its own cyanobacterium in a completely separate event about 90-140 million years ago, and its captive's genome has already shrunk to a third of its free-living relatives' -- a second run of the same experiment, caught in progress. T10 (the honest caveat): Margulis was right about mitochondria and chloroplasts and NOT right about everything -- her claim that cilia and flagella descend from spirochete bacteria has never been supported, and the bank says so. T11: most of the swallowed bacterium's genes did not vanish, they MOVED -- transferred into the host's nucleus, which is why the organelle can no longer survive on its own.
source: Grokipedia: Lynn Margulis, Symbiogenesis, Endosymbiont, Chloroplast, Organelle, Archaea, Loki's Castle, Two-domain system; Wikipedia: Lynn Margulis, Symbiogenesis, Paulinella, Promethearchaeum; Sagan (Margulis), 'On the Origin of Mitosing Cells', J. Theor. Biol. 1967; Imachi et al., Nature 2020 (Prometheoarchaeum/MK-D1); Spang et al. 2015 (Lokiarchaeota).
framing_note: Flagship REVERSAL for the sub-strand: a rejected outsider's claim became the thing every textbook now teaches -- consensus is not evidence, and the EVIDENCE rungs (T2, T3, T4) are what won it, not persistence alone. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) she published as Lynn Sagan in 1967 -- name it right; (2) 'about fifteen journals' is her own recollection, so keep the word 'about'; (3) do not sanctify her -- T10 exists so the ladder shows a real scientist being right and wrong in the same theory. Dinner-test payoff: T1. Anti-restatement: the evidence rungs must not restate 'because they were once bacteria' in the stem -- give the observation (a DNA loop, a 70S ribosome) and let the inference be recalled. Distractor mine: the genuine rival explanation of the era (organelles formed by the cell's own membrane folding inward -- the autogenous hypothesis), plus Lamarckism, Mereschkowski and Wallin as real adjacent names.
history_overlap: ANIMAL bank owns creature-level symbiosis (clownfish and anemone, gut microbes of ruminants, coral and zooxanthellae) -- this ladder stays on the ORGANELLE and its molecular evidence and must not drift into partnership-between-animals territory.

name: How small is small -- and why cells stay that way
scope: A CONCEPT ladder on scale, with a counting reversal at its centre. T1 (invert the wonder): a human hair is about 70 micrometres across -- which means you could lay only about three to seven of your own cells side by side to span one hair, and about five hundred bacteria the size of E. coli across the same hair. T2: you are made of roughly thirty to thirty-seven trillion cells (Bianconi's 2013 count: 37.2 trillion; Sender and Milo's 2016 revision: about 30 trillion) -- and the overwhelming majority of them are red blood cells, which are tiny, disc-shaped and have thrown their nucleus away. T3 (the reversal): 'you are only ten percent human' was in textbooks and TED talks for forty years, traced back to a single back-of-the-envelope estimate by Thomas Luckey in 1972. In 2016 Sender, Fuchs and Milo simply redid the arithmetic: about 38 trillion bacteria to about 30 trillion human cells -- roughly 1.3 to 1, not 10 to 1 -- and the entire microbiome weighs only around 0.2 kg, not the widely repeated kilograms. A myth killed by careful counting, with no new instrument involved. T4 (the mechanism, and the kid-test): a cell's food comes in through its surface and feeds its whole volume -- double a cube's width and its volume grows eightfold while its surface grows only fourfold, so big cells starve in the middle. You can watch it: cubes of dyed agar or gelatin of different sizes dropped in vinegar or bleach, sliced open after the same number of minutes, show the colour front reaching the middle of the small cube and nowhere near the middle of the big one. T5 (the exception that proves the rule): Thiomargarita magnifica, found growing on sunken red mangrove leaves in Guadeloupe and described in 2022, is a SINGLE bacterium up to 2 cm long -- visible without any microscope at all. It cheats: a vast vacuole fills 65-80 percent of it and squeezes the living cytoplasm into a thin shell against the surface, and its DNA sits packed in membrane-bound sacs called pepins rather than loose. T6: E. coli splits about every twenty minutes in ideal broth, which is why one cell becomes a visible colony overnight -- and why nothing in nature ever gets ideal broth for long. T7: the biggest single cell most people have held is an ostrich egg yolk; the longest cell in you is a nerve cell running from the base of your spine to your toe.
source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, 'Revised Estimates for the Number of Human and Bacteria Cells in the Body', PLOS Biology 14(8):e1002533, 2016; Bianconi et al., 'An estimation of the number of cells in the human body', Annals of Human Biology 40(6), 2013; Wikipedia: Thiomargarita magnifica, Human microbiome; Volland et al. 2022 (Science) on T. magnifica; Grokipedia: Bacteria, Cell (biology).
framing_note: INVERT-THE-WONDER throughout plus one REVERSAL (T3) that is pure bank voice -- an expert-endorsed number repeated for decades, corrected by someone bothering to check the arithmetic. THE ACCURACY RAIL: the popular line 'a cell is to an apple as an apple is to the Earth' is FALSE and must not be used -- that ratio belongs to the ATOM/apple/Earth comparison (magnify an apple to Earth size and its atoms become apple-sized); a cell blown up by the same factor would be kilometres wide. Use hair-widths and the cited counts instead. Second rail: re-verify the red-blood-cell share (about 84 percent, Sender 2016) at build time before writing a rung on it. Dinner-test payoff: T3 and T5. Distractor mine: the discarded numbers themselves -- 10:1, 'a hundred trillion cells', '1-2 kg of gut bacteria' -- all real published figures, which is exactly why they are fair distractors.
history_overlap: ANIMAL bank owns ostrich and egg facts as creature facts -- if the T7 egg rung survives, it must key the SINGLE-CELL claim about the yolk, not anything about the bird.

name: HeLa: the cells that outlived Henrietta Lacks
scope: The most useful cells in the world, and the woman nobody asked. T1: on 8 February 1951 a biopsy was taken at Johns Hopkins from a 31-year-old tobacco farmer named Henrietta Lacks; she was dead of cervical cancer by that October, and her cells are still dividing in laboratories on every continent more than seventy years later. T2: George Gey's lab had spent decades failing to keep any human cells alive in glass -- these doubled roughly every twenty-four hours and would not stop; he named the line HeLa from the first two letters of each of her names, and gave samples away free to anyone who asked. T3 (the mechanism): the reason they never stop is that human papillomavirus 18 DNA had inserted itself into her tumour cells and left telomerase switched permanently on -- the cells rebuild their own chromosome end-caps after every division and simply skip the countdown that stops normal cells. T4: their first great job was Jonas Salk's polio vaccine -- HeLa cells visibly died when polio infected them, which made a readable yes/no test -- and demand was so enormous that a HeLa mass-production centre was set up at the Tuskegee Institute in 1953. T5 (the flip side): HeLa is a weed. Stanley Gartler's mid-1960s finding, later confirmed again and again, showed that a great many supposedly distinct human cell lines in the world's laboratories were secretly HeLa contaminants -- years of published results about 'liver cells' or 'breast cells' were actually about Henrietta Lacks's cervical cancer. T6 (the consent rung): in 1951 no law and no hospital rule required asking a patient about leftover surgical tissue -- so nothing illegal happened, and her family still knew nothing at all until 1973, when researchers turned up wanting their blood for genetic studies. T7: in 2013 a team published the full HeLa genome -- her family's inherited information -- without asking them; the NIH and the Lacks family then negotiated a controlled-access arrangement giving family representatives a seat on the review board, and in August 2023 Thermo Fisher settled the estate's lawsuit over selling HeLa products. T8 (the honest ledger): HeLa appears in tens of thousands of papers, flew in the early space programme, and underpinned the work linking HPV to cervical cancer that produced the vaccine -- the good is enormous and real, and so is the wrong done to her family; the bank reports both and does not resolve them for the reader.
source: Grokipedia: HeLa, Henrietta Lacks, George Otto Gey, Immortalised cell line, The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks; Wikipedia: HeLa; Rebecca Skloot, The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks (2010) for the family narrative and the NIH negotiation; NIH 2013 HeLa Genome Data Use Agreement announcement; Gartler's cell-line cross-contamination reports (mid-1960s).
framing_note: Tell it straight, both ledgers, no villain cartoon and no whitewash -- the bank PRESENTS and lets a father and child argue about it at the table. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) the biopsy was taken by Dr Lawrence Wharton Jr; Gey received the sample, he did not take it; (2) obtaining consent for leftover tissue was not legally required in 1951, and the honest statement is BOTH that nothing then-illegal occurred AND that the family was shut out of decisions and profits for decades; (3) date Gartler's contamination bombshell as 'the mid-1960s' rather than pinning a single year. Dinner-test payoff: T1. Anti-restatement: T3's stem gives the observation (these cells never stop) and the mechanism is recalled, not spelled out. Distractor mine: other real immortal or famous lines (WI-38, Vero, CHO) and other real names (Gey, Salk, Gartler). vision_mandated TRUE: this is an institutional-failure and consent topic where the bank's stance -- report the wrong plainly, and report the benefit plainly -- has to be built in at authoring time, not patched in audit.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank owns the Tuskegee syphilis study and civil-rights-era medical ethics. The Tuskegee Institute HeLa production factory (1953) is a DIFFERENT thing from the Tuskegee syphilis study and must be labelled unambiguously if used; do not retell the syphilis study in this ladder.

name: The immortal chicken heart that wasn't
scope: A famous result that would not replicate, and the internal clock that replaced it. T1: for thirty-four years a scrap of chicken heart tissue was fed daily at the Rockefeller Institute and its birthdays were reported in the newspapers -- Alexis Carrel's culture was the celebrated proof that cells, given good food, never age at all. Nobody has ever reproduced it. T2: in 1961 Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead found the opposite -- normal human cells divide roughly forty to sixty times and then stop dividing and just sit there, alive but finished; the field's response was that they must have been sloppy. T3 (the trick that settled it): to prove it was not the food or the glassware, they MIXED male cells that had already gone through forty doublings with female cells that had gone through only fifteen, in one flask sharing everything -- twenty doublings later, only female cells were left. Whatever was counting was inside each cell. T4: the likely explanation for Carrel's immortal culture is embarrassingly ordinary -- the embryo extract fed to it daily was probably smuggling in fresh living cells, so the culture never aged because it was never the same cells. T5 (the mechanism): the counter is the telomere, the repeated sequence capping each chromosome, which loses a little length at every copy; Alexei Olovnikov predicted exactly this in 1971 from how DNA copying ends, and Carol Greider and Elizabeth Blackburn found telomerase, the enzyme that rebuilds the caps, in 1984 -- Nobel in 2009. T6: cancer cells cheat by switching telomerase back on, which is precisely why HeLa cells never stop -- the same fact seen from the other side. T7: the phenomenon carries Hayflick's name because Macfarlane Burnet christened it the Hayflick limit in a 1974 book, well after the result had stopped being controversial.
source: Wikipedia: Hayflick limit, Leonard Hayflick, Alexis Carrel, Telomerase; Hayflick & Moorhead, Exp. Cell Res. 1961; Greider & Blackburn, Cell 1985 (telomerase, work of 1984); Nobel Prize 2009 physiology/medicine citation; Grokipedia: Immortalised cell line, Senescence.
framing_note: REVERSAL plus a corrected misconception, and one of the cleanest 'how would you rule out the alternative?' rungs in the sub-strand. ACCURACY RAIL: do NOT accuse Carrel of fraud -- the documented position is that the result was never replicated and was most likely sustained by fresh cells arriving in the daily embryo extract; 'probably contaminated, not proven faked' is the honest wording. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the mixed flask). Anti-restatement: T3's stem describes the mixed culture and the outcome without naming 'an internal counter' -- that is the answer. Distractor mine: the genuinely live alternatives of the time -- the medium ran out of something, waste products accumulated, the glass was contaminated, cells die from external wear -- plus Carrel and Weismann as real adjacent names.

name: Stem cells: one cell that can become any
scope: How you prove an invisible cell exists, and how the one-way door was pushed back open. T1: in 1961 in Toronto, James Till and Ernest McCulloch injected bone marrow into mice whose own marrow had been destroyed by radiation, and days later found small raised LUMPS on the spleens -- and the number of lumps went up in proportion to the number of cells injected, which meant you could count something nobody could see. T2: each lump grew from a SINGLE cell -- proved in 1963 with Andy Becker by using radiation-scarred chromosomes as unique markers -- and each lump contained several kinds of blood cell plus more cells that could start the whole process again: the two properties that define a stem cell. T3: in 1962 John Gurdon took the nucleus out of a tadpole's gut cell, put it into a frog egg whose own nucleus had been destroyed, and got a swimming tadpole -- meaning a specialised cell still carries the complete instructions for building a whole animal; specialisation is not deletion. T4: Gurdon's Eton schoolmaster had written of him, in a report he later framed and hung in his office, 'I believe he has ideas about becoming a scientist; on his present showing this is quite ridiculous.' T5: in 2006 Shinya Yamanaka started with twenty-four genes active in embryonic cells, put them all into adult mouse skin cells, then removed them one at a time to see which ones mattered -- and got down to FOUR (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc) that reset an adult cell to an embryo-like state; he and Gurdon shared the 2012 Nobel. T6 (what specialising costs): Conrad Waddington's 1957 picture is a marble rolling down a hillside of branching valleys -- gravity does the specialising for free, and getting back to the hilltop is the thing Gurdon and Yamanaka had to force. T7 (the skepticism rung): in 2014 a spectacular claim that a mild acid bath could reprogram cells -- STAP cells -- filled the front pages, could not be replicated by anyone, and was retracted after a misconduct finding; and today unlicensed clinics worldwide sell 'stem cell cures' that have never passed a trial. Exciting is not the same as true. T8: the treatment that genuinely works is old and unglamorous -- a bone marrow transplant is a stem cell transplant, developed by E. Donnall Thomas and colleagues from the 1950s onward.
source: Wikipedia: James Till, Ernest McCulloch, John Gurdon, Induced pluripotent stem cell, STAP cell; Till & McCulloch, Radiation Research 1961; Becker, McCulloch & Till, Nature 1963; Gurdon, J. Embryol. Exp. Morphol. 1962; Takahashi & Yamanaka, Cell 2006; Nobel Prize 2012 citation; Waddington, The Strategy of the Genes, 1957.
framing_note: DISCOVERY mode with the bank's skepticism virtue built in at T7 -- the same ladder that celebrates a breakthrough shows a breakthrough that collapsed, which is the point. ACCURACY RAIL: Gurdon's 1962 result was doubted for a real reason -- he could not then prove the donor nucleus came from a FULLY differentiated cell, and the airtight demonstration came in 1975; say this rather than presenting 1962 as instantly accepted. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the framed school report) with T1 as the mechanism payoff. Anti-restatement: T1's stem gives the lumps and the proportionality; the conclusion (a countable stem cell) is the answer. Distractor mine: real adjacent milestones that are the WRONG answer here -- Dolly and Ian Wilmut (1996), James Thomson's human embryonic stem cells (1998), Steward's carrot-cell work -- plus the retracted STAP claim as a live-looking option on the reprogramming rung.

name: The filter that caught nothing: what a virus is
scope: An agent too small to catch, and a question still unanswered. T1: in 1892 Dmitri Ivanovsky pressed sap from mosaic-diseased tobacco plants through an unglazed porcelain filter with pores too fine for any known bacterium to pass -- and the filtered, supposedly sterile juice still gave healthy plants the disease. T2: Ivanovsky himself assumed he had a toxin or a bacterium small enough to slip through; it was Martinus Beijerinck in 1898 who repeated the filtration, showed the agent MULTIPLIED, but only inside living plant tissue, and called it contagium vivum fluidum -- a living contagious fluid. A poison cannot make more of itself. T3: in 1935 Wendell Stanley purified tobacco mosaic virus into needle-like CRYSTALS -- a bottle of dry crystals that could sit on a shelf like table salt -- and when he redissolved them they infected plants as vigorously as ever. T4 (mechanism): a virus has no ribosomes and runs no metabolism of its own; it is instructions wrapped in a protein coat, and it does nothing at all until it gets inside a cell and borrows that cell's machinery. T5 (the MYSTERY rung): so is a virus alive? There is no settled answer -- serious biologists divide on it, the definitions of life were written before viruses were known, and the bank says plainly that nobody has resolved it. T6: in 1992 something in the water of a Bradford cooling tower was found inside amoebae, took up a Gram stain, and was filed away as a bacterium -- until 2003, when it was identified as mimivirus, a virus with 1.18 million bases of DNA and about a thousand genes, including protein-building genes that viruses were not supposed to have. It had been misfiled for eleven years because it was too big to be a virus. T7: virus particles outnumber every other biological entity on Earth, and marine bacteriophages kill a substantial share of the ocean's bacteria every single day -- the biggest predator on the planet is one you cannot see.
source: Grokipedia: Virus, Virology, History of virology, Dmitri Ivanovsky, Tobacco mosaic virus, Introduction to viruses; Wikipedia: Mimivirus; Stanley, Science 1935; Beijerinck 1898; La Scola et al., Science 2003 (mimivirus identification).
framing_note: MYSTERY plus MECHANISM. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) Ivanovsky ran the experiment but did NOT make the conceptual leap -- he suspected a toxin or a very small bacterium, and Beijerinck supplied the new category; a stem crediting Ivanovsky with 'discovering viruses' as a new form of agent is wrong; (2) on the alive-or-not rung, no distractor may secretly be the true answer -- the honest option (unresolved) must be the correct one. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a living thing you can crystallise in a jar). Distractor mine: the two real historical readings of the filtered sap (a chemical poison, a tiny bacterium), plus Pasteur's filterable rabies agent and Loeffler and Frosch's foot-and-mouth work as real adjacent claims.
history_overlap: The science bank's disease/epidemic sub-strand owns vaccines and outbreaks (Jenner, smallpox, polio) -- this ladder keys the FILTER and the nature of a virus, not disease history. Salk and polio are already used in the HeLa ladder; keep them out of this one.

name: Abbe's wall: the limit that had to be dodged, not broken
scope: A CONCEPT ladder on the physics of seeing small things, carrying the sub-strand's analytic ceiling. T1: for two centuries better microscopes meant better glass -- until Ernst Abbe worked out in 1873 that the blur has nothing to do with craftsmanship. Light is a wave, and two things closer than roughly half its wavelength -- about 200 nanometres for visible light -- cannot be separated by ANY lens, however perfectly ground. A wall made of physics, not skill. T2: what that wall hid: a virus, a ribosome, and the gap between two nerve cells all sit on the wrong side of 200 nm, so for sixty years they were not small and blurry, they were simply unseeable. T3: Ernst Ruska's answer in 1931-33 was to stop using light -- electrons behave as waves too, with wavelengths thousands of times shorter, and his electron microscope beat the best light microscope within two years; his Nobel came fifty-odd years later, in 1986. T4 (the honest trade-off): electron microscopy buys resolution with life -- the specimen sits in a vacuum, dried, usually killed and coated in metal, so the sharpest pictures of a cell are pictures of a corpse. T5 (the dodge): Stefan Hell's STED keeps ordinary light and cheats the rules instead -- a second, doughnut-shaped beam switches OFF the glowing molecules around the rim of the spot so only the molecules in the tiny dark centre report back; the diffraction limit is untouched, but the region actually emitting is far smaller than it. T6: Eric Betzig and W.E. Moerner attacked it the other way -- let one lone molecule glow at a time, and although its image is a fat 250 nm blur, the CENTRE of that blur can be computed to a few nanometres; do that thousands of times and the dots draw a picture no lens could form. Nobel in Chemistry, 2014. T7: cryo-electron microscopy (Nobel 2017, Dubochet, Frank and Henderson) froze the trade-off away -- plunge the sample so fast that its water becomes glass instead of ice crystals, and a molecule can be imaged close to the shape it holds in life.
source: Wikipedia: Super-resolution microscopy, Diffraction-limited system, Ernst Abbe, Ernst Ruska, Cryogenic electron microscopy; Nobel Prize citations 1986 (physics), 2014 (chemistry), 2017 (chemistry); Grokipedia: Microscopy, Microscope, Timeline of microscope technology.
framing_note: MECHANISM mode, and a precision test for the bank's own honesty. THE ACCURACY RAIL: super-resolution does NOT break or violate Abbe's diffraction limit -- the limit still holds for the light being collected; what changed is control over WHICH molecules emit at a given instant. Every headline says 'broke the limit'; the bank must say it correctly, and that gap is itself worth a rung. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the doughnut that switches off the outside). Teach-before-test: wavelength and resolution must be set up in an earlier rung before any rung leans on them. Distractor mine: the intuitive-but-wrong fixes -- grind a better lens, use a stronger lamp, magnify more -- which is exactly what everyone tried before Abbe, plus Zernike's phase contrast and confocal microscopy as real adjacent techniques that do NOT beat the limit.
